title: Benefit party for Shake Up Melindsay and the trumpeters' contest; origin of Panama
summary: Broussard recalls a benefit party where Sam Morgan, Kid Rena, Punch, Philip Moreri and others competed, and says a part of his childhood Albert Blues went into Panama.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: I mean, you can... I'll tell you about this Shake Up Melindsay fellow. That's what I was going to tell you one time about Shake Up Melindsay. I'll come to meet him. He had gotten sick, see? So all the musicians, they got together and they decided that they would give a party and it all pay for nothing. And they would give, you know, all the proceeds to him. So that's how I come to meet Shake Up Melindsay. What part of town did he come from? He, I think he came from across the river someplace. I didn't know too much of him. But his mother had just lately moved next door to us. I think she had bought the house, see? But before that, they had came from across the river, I think. And so they gave the party. And at that party, they had a whole gang of trumpet players there. And you would have enjoyed hearing that. And these was the trumpeters that they had there. They had Sam Morgan. They had Kid Rainy. They had Shake Up Melindsay. They had Punch. They had Philip Moreri. Philip Moreri, he played there. Now that was a guy. He's the guy that played Panama. He's the guy composed at Panama. And he got killed. He was trying to hold boys the way to Chicago. That's the way. Because he was going up that way to, that's the way that most of the guys, you know, they didn't make much money. And if they had any way of getting someplace with their instruments or their horn, they'd get there. If it was danger, they didn't mind danger. They was going to get there. See? And he got killed. And his trumpet was crushed inside of him. But he was the guy who played this number, Panama. And if they check up on it, you ain't going to never find the fellow who composed Panama. Because he was the guy, because I had put some part of the lyrics, I mean the music to it, because he liked it, that part that was one of the numbers that I made when I was a little kid. I was about, oh, I was about, about nine then. And I had composed a little blues. And I called it Albert Blues, because my name is Albert Broussard, see? And he used a part of those blues to put in Panama. And I remember well that they said he had composed that music because there was a piano player. Oh, he was much of a piano player. They called him Cross-Eyed George for a nickname. I don't know what his real name is. I think his name was George Harris. I think it was Harris. But they called him Cross-Eyed George. And oh, he could play a piano. And Phillip Moreri was playing along with him when I first heard him. Well, Phillip Moreri was one of the guys that was at the party. And it was all contests. And that's where the joy came in. When he would hit that high note, when he was playing Panama, he'd go way down there. And he'd say he had that number. Ta-da! Ta-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da! And he'd just keep that note over and over. And it was really thrilling to hear him play that number. And then this fellow Punch would blow the same number because they had all gotten into it because it was really a good number. And they all had a little piece of that number, but he had a master. See? He didn't have the reputation that they had because he was a newcomer then. But he was making it warm for them. And he was sitting down there enjoying it and everybody was over there and he was just a youngster. He was blowing up some trumpet. I mean, our judge at that time, Phillip must have been about 19 years old, 19 or 20 years old. They called him Phillip Moreri. And he played much piano. And that's why I heard Shake Up My Lens. And when he got to make it warm, then he came there with that number. Ta-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. And that was his main number with Shake Up My Lens. And that's where I had first saw some of the good musicians. And Ory was there. And he was a trombone player at that time. And who else was there? And I can't think of this other trumpet. Oh, yeah. Cabone. Frank Cabone was there. He was the guy. He played music on progressive jazz now. He was always a half note in front of the music that you was playing. But the way that he played it, oh, man, he was really strong with it. He only died recently. He was one of my uncles. What was the name again? Frank Thompson. Frank Thompson. Frank Thompson. Now, he played quite a few jobs around his town. He really, he had cornbread quite a lot. And he had Big Al. Do you know Big Al? Oh, yeah. Big Al. Guitar player? Yeah, guitar player. Well, Big Al and him, Big Al used to play guitar for him.
